https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/tech.text: You decide to learn something because it catches your attention, and for a while that is enough. Then curiosity gets audited: Is there a course? A certificate? A LinkedIn post? Can it become content? When no obvious payoff appears, the interest starts looking embarrassingly useless. Some of the people we now celebrate followed questions long before the outcome was visible. Einstein kept returning to a compass; Frida Kahlo to the face in her mirror. Neither knew where the fascination would lead. They simply stayed with it long enough for curiosity to become something larger.Is Instagram teaching us what to be curious about?Instagram has a new aspiration for us: become âdisgustingly educatedâ. Creators recommend books and subjects, and the advice is hard to quarrel with if it gets people reading. More curious is that we needed Instagram to tell us to be curious.A 2009 Psychological Science study by Min Jeong Kang and colleagues asked a simple question: what happens when you really want to know the answer? Participants rated how curious they were about trivia questions, and the more curious they were, the more activity researchers saw in parts of the brain linked to anticipating rewards. People were even willing to spend limited tokens or wait longer for answers they particularly wanted. Curiosity also helped the information stick; participants were more likely to remember answers later when they had been genuinely curious about them in the first place. In other words, the answer itself had become a reward.People who were highly curious about one answer also remembered unrelated information they happened to encounter while waiting for it. A 2014 Neuron study from UC Davis found that this extra material stayed with participants more easily, even though it had nothing to do with the original question. Brain scans also showed greater activity in regions involved in reward and memory during these high-curiosity moments. Curiosity, the researchers found, can prime the brain to absorb more than the thing it originally set out to learn.When does a useless question become useful?What would make a five-year-old keep thinking about a compass long after the novelty should have worn off? For Albert Einstein, the mystery was the invisible force pulling the needle north. The American Museum of Natural History notes that this fascination opened into a much wider interest in science, followed by books on mathematics and geometry. Years later, he was asking what he might see if he could travel alongside a beam of light. At what point does a childâs question become serious intellectual work? Usually, only in hindsight.Shakespeare gives us a harder case because we cannot recover his private curiosity so neatly. What we can see is the sheer range of material that entered his plays. Folger scholars have traced Virgil and Ovid through his work, along with Plutarch, Holinshedâs Chronicles and the Bible. He wrote for paying audiences and became a wealthy man, yet his reading kept spilling across history, mythology and politics. If Shakespeare had treated knowledge only as material for the next commission, would his work have ranged as widely as it did?Picture an 18-year-old who had planned to study medicine, suddenly confined to bed after a bus accident. With a mirror fixed above her and paints within reach, she began studying the face staring back at her, first because there was time to fill and then because painting gave her something to keep pursuing. The self-portraits came before anyone could know what they would become. The young woman was Frida Kahlo, and the work that now seems inseparable from her identity began as an interest she followed without any guarantee that it would lead anywhere.In Warsaw, a young woman kept studying science even when the universities around her would not admit women. She learnt physics and chemistry from her father, worked for years as a governess to support herself and eventually moved to Paris to study mathematics and physics at the Sorbonne. Later, a question raised by Henri Becquerelâs work on uranium pulled her deeper into research: what exactly was producing those strange rays? Marie Curie followed that question far enough to discover polonium and radium, but none of that was visible at the beginning. Long before two Nobel Prizes made the story look inevitable, there was simply curiosity and the decision to keep following it.Have we become too impatient to be bad at things?While trend can get you started, the real trouble begins when the book gets boring. Learning usually includes a stretch in which you are confused, slow and unimpressive, with little evidence that all this effort is leading anywhere. Anyone who has wrestled with a difficult subject knows how long that stretch can last.Tanmay Sinha and Manu Kapur looked at what happens when learners get the problem before the lesson. Their 2021 meta-analysis covered 53 studies and 166 comparisons between problem-solving-first and instruction-first approaches. Students who tried the problem first performed better overall, with stronger effects when researchers followed the principles of Kapurâs âproductive failureâ closely. Wrong turns exposed what learners did not understand, giving the later instruction something to work with.This middle stage is poor material for a progress post. A finished book is easy to photograph; the week in which you reread the same three pages because the argument keeps slipping away is less cooperative. Much of the learning happens there anyway.What happens when you have to choose the next question yourself?The useful part of the âdisgustingly educatedâ trend probably begins when you stop following it properly. A recommended book sends you towards someone you have never heard of, one reference opens another subject and the original list quietly becomes irrelevant. At some point, you are no longer learning because Instagram suggested it; you are still there because something has started bothering you enough to keep looking.A recommendation can get you through the door; curiosity decides whether you wander off once you are inside. Once you have wandered off, there is no prize for returning to the list on time. Next time something catches your interest, follow it before you can talk yourself out of it.You use AI every day.
